Banking & Accountability

Six Words Inside Frankfurt: How Revenue Outran the Rules at Deutsche Bank

Fifteen million leaked Deutsche Bank documents describe an institution where compliance was a cost centre and revenue was the point.

Reported by Roger

More than fifty newsrooms began publishing this week from a cache of fifteen million internal Deutsche Bank documents—nine million of them emails—handed to journalists Josy Joseph and Khadija Sharife by two whistleblowers [s544]. The files come from the units tasked with catching money laundering, sanctions violations, and reputational risk, and they depict a bank where those checks routinely lost to the bottom line [s544].

"KYC bricht uns das revenue Genick."

Those six words—written in a 2017 email by Christian Sewing, who became chief executive the following year—translate to "Know Your Customer breaks our revenue neck" [s544]. According to the reporting, Jeffrey Epstein's accounts generated roughly $600 million in suspicious transactions before the bank closed his last accounts in July 2019, while in 2020 an employee stumbled upon a laundering network that individual surveillance systems had flagged in pieces for three years without connecting [s544].

Since 2008, Deutsche Bank has paid more than 20 billion euros in fines and settlements against a 1.4-trillion-euro balance sheet—a sum that functioned less as a deterrent than as a licensing fee [s544].

Security & Infrastructure

Phala Warns of Exposed Inference VM; Luxor Details Mining Fleet Breach

Two separate infrastructure disclosures put OpenRouter users and bitcoin miners on notice to rotate credentials and audit payouts.

In this week's issue of Attested, aljaz flagged Phala's preliminary incident report warning that an attacker could see in-flight requests on one unhardened inference VM [s534]. Users whose OpenRouter DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests were routed to Phala between October 21 and November 8 are advised to treat them as exposed and rotate any keys, tokens, or passwords [s534].

Separately, 4plus17 reported on a Sunday-night breach of Luxor's Commander fleet-management software, in which attackers reconfigured mining hardware across roughly a dozen customer accounts to point at OCEAN and their own payout addresses [s535]. Luxor closed the gap within two hours and pledged to compensate affected customers [s535].
